section_1.title: The Bridge: From Geometry to Abstraction (1 min)
section_1.content: Transition from Euclidean vectors (arrows in 2D/3D space) to abstract vectors. Define a vector space not by 'what it looks like' (arrows), but by 'how it behaves' (the 8 axioms of addition and scalar multiplication).
section_1.example: Visualizing a 'vector' as a simple arrow shifting from (0,0) to (3,2) vs. a vector that is actually a complex function, like f(x) = x².

section_2.title: Defining the 'Rules of the Game' (1.5 min)
section_2.content: Introduce the core requirements: Closure under addition and scalar multiplication. Use a graphical checklist animation where any set that breaks these rules is 'crossed out' and rejected from being a vector space.
section_2.example: Scenario: A 'Robot Factory' where the robots (vectors) must always be able to combine (add) and be scaled (multiplied) to remain valid robots. If combining two robots creates a 'glitch' (leaves the set), the set fails the closure test.

section_3.title: Diverse Examples: Functions as Vectors (1.5 min)
section_3.content: Demonstrate that vectors are just 'elements' that obey the rules. Show that polynomials of degree ≤ 2 form a vector space. Visualize this by treating a parabola as a single point in a higher-dimensional 'function space'.
section_3.example: Imagine a 'Digital Pet' evolution. A pet is defined by its traits. Adding two pets (traits) results in a new, valid pet within the same species-space. This shows how mathematical abstraction mirrors biological variation.

section_4.title: Summary & Synthesis (1 min)
section_4.content: Recap: An abstract vector space is a container of objects where we can perform linear combinations. Reiterate that the 'arrows' were just a specific, intuitive realization of a much broader, powerful algebraic concept.
section_4.example: Final Animation: A zoom-out view showing that arrows, matrices, and functions are all just different 'shapes' living inside the same 'Vector Space' skyscraper.
